rows.text: Listening to your answers yesterday to the Welsh Affairs Committee, you mentioned that the appointment of a new chief content officer would be made by the new chief executive.

rows.speaker: Tom Giffard
rows.text: So, can you help me understand why the termination of the employment would be handled by the chair but the appointment would be handled by a chief executive?

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: Because, quite simply, the circumstances that led to the dismissal of the chief content officer occurred on a Saturday in Nantes, following a rugby match.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: The chief executive had attended the same meetings—well, they weren't meetings—but the chief executive was present at the same locations where these events took place, which led to that decision.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: So, the chief executive had an interest in that issue.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: She hadn't shared that with anyone within S4C, although the wider industry in Wales all knew what had been said and to whom.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: It was being reported in the press almost before we'd heard about these events.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: So, under those circumstances, and having receiving advice on procedure and on employment law and the appropriate steps to be taken, I took the decision that action had to be taken immediately in order to safeguard the reputation of S4C.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: As was mentioned earlier, I have been in this business for many years and have never come across a case of a senior official behaving in that way.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: If the new chief executive were to decide—.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: Of course, they will appoint somebody, whether that person will be a chief content officer or a director of content or a director of programming—there are all sorts of possible titles.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: When a new chief executive appoints, I would expect, as it happens, that the chair, whoever he or she may be, would be invited into that process.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: I was involved in the process of appointing Llinos Griffin-Williams to S4C, because the post was one of those posts that carries the additional duties of being an executive director of the shadow unitary board.

rows.speaker: Chris Jones
rows.text: Could I just add on that point very briefly, Chair?

rows.speaker: Delyth Jewell
rows.text: Very briefly, yes.

rows.speaker: Chris Jones
rows.text: I think the key point, as Rhodri has described, is the fact that this was an extremely unusual situation and there was a perceived need to act extremely quickly, which is why the chair, with external legal advice, set in place a process for those unique circumstances.

rows.speaker: Chris Jones
rows.text: So, it would not be the normal way that that would be handled.

rows.speaker: Chris Jones
rows.text: Indeed, I referred earlier to the fact that there was robust debate amongst directors, but that the non-executive directors were not able to be involved in that process because of the timescale.

rows.speaker: Chris Jones
rows.text: That was also something that was then discussed after the event, because that was very unusual.

rows.speaker: Chris Jones
rows.text: Had there been a way to have had a wider process, then that would clearly have been beneficial, but the view taken by the chair, with external specialist advice, was that the circumstances and the need to act so quickly justified taking that unusual process.

rows.speaker: Chris Jones
rows.text: But you're right, that's not how you would normally go about it.

rows.speaker: Tom Giffard
rows.text: Just very finally from me on the appointment of a new chief executive, you've mentioned that there's no real time frame on that appointment yet.

rows.speaker: Tom Giffard
rows.text: Is it your intention that that will happen in the remainder of your term?

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: I think the board will be discussing that—

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: Sorry, I don't know why I turned to English there.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: The board will discuss that a fortnight today.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: In terms of how far we could go, I wouldn't think that an appointment would be made, if I'm perfectly honest, during the remainder of my term of office; I wouldn't expect it to happen within that period.

rows.speaker: Delyth Jewell
rows.text: Thank you.

rows.speaker: Delyth Jewell
rows.text: We're very aware of how long you've stayed with us—thank you very much.

rows.speaker: Delyth Jewell
rows.text: I have two very brief questions, at the end.

rows.speaker: Delyth Jewell
rows.text: You mentioned to Alun, and this was raised yesterday, that you'd asked for many meetings with DCMS and that that hadn't happened.

rows.speaker: Delyth Jewell
rows.text: Do you think it's appropriate, therefore, that it's the Secretary of State who has the powers in this situation if the Secretary of State doesn't show an interest in having a meeting?

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: I think that's beyond my responsibilities in terms of expressing a view on who should—.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: In other words, that's the framework that we're working within—

rows.speaker: Delyth Jewell
rows.text: But perhaps the framework isn't working as well as it should at the moment.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: As I said, we have occasionally met with some Ministers from the department, but as I said, when I proposed that we should meet the Secretary of State to discuss this specific issue, as it happens, that offer was not accepted.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: It appears to me that when this process was ongoing, there wasn't a great deal of interest shown in it, but because of the way things have panned out—and that isn't how I would have imagined things developing when this whole process started—everyone, now, is taking an interest in all aspects of this.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: That's to be expected, isn't it?

rows.speaker: Delyth Jewell
rows.text: Thank you.

rows.speaker: Delyth Jewell
rows.text: Just the final question: is there anything that you regret about the whole situation?

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: Yes.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: I regret this point that we've been discussing that we as a board weren't aware of these concerns at an earlier stage.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: I do regret, with hindsight, that the remit that we agreed with Capital Law was one that allowed the process to take a long period of time.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: There were reasons for that.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: Because of this fear factor that I have referred to, that was a very important part of drawing up the remit in very broad terms that, of course, then allowed everyone to contribute to this process.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: So, in a way, we created a problem for ourselves.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: The BECTU complaint didn't refer to the board or to governance; it related to the management team, as it was referred to, although not every member of that management team was involved, but they couldn't be specific about complaints, and it wouldn't have been appropriate to name individuals in that scenario.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: BECTU had been very careful in that regard.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: But, of course, that did mean that the process was lengthier and that the process did allow people who were the subjects of complaints to be contributing to it.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: I do believe that it would have been more beneficial, perhaps, for our staff and for the mental health of our staff throughout this period, if we had agreed a remit that focused more on what BECTU were complaining about, rather than saying, 'Come to us to talk about anything that's on your mind.'

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: But, with the information that we had at the time, I was quite content that we needed to put a process in place that was very open, in order to ensure that people had the confidence to contribute to it.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: But do I regret that now?

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: Yes.

rows.speaker: Delyth Jewell
rows.text: Thank you.

rows.speaker: Delyth Jewell
rows.text: We're very grateful for the additional time you've provided this afternoon.

rows.speaker: Delyth Jewell
rows.text: There will be a transcript of the meeting sent to you to ensure that it's a fair reflection of what's been said, and perhaps there will be some technical questions that we haven't been able to ask, and we'll want to write to you about those.

rows.speaker: Delyth Jewell
rows.text: But thank you very much for being with us this afternoon.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: Thank you all very much for your time and for the way in which you have questioned us this afternoon.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: I have said in this committee previously that do we appreciate and are always willing to be held to account by you as elected Members.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: Despite the fact that the circumstances are unpleasant, I am grateful for the way in which you have asked your questions and have dealt with us today.

rows.speaker: Rhodri Williams
rows.text: Thank you very much.

rows.speaker: Delyth Jewell
rows.text: Thank you very much.
